Three weeks after Noa ended it, Nadia still picked up her phone every night in her Lisbon flat to text her. Noa had been kind but clear: she wanted to move to Berlin for good, and Nadia wanted to stay near her mother, who was getting older. Neither of them was wrong. That was the hardest part.
Nadia's friend Inês made her write two lists: what she loved about Noa, and what she needed in a partner. The second list surprised her. Staying near family was on it. So was someone who talked about plans, not just feelings.
She deleted the draft messages. On Sundays she started running by the river again with Inês, slow and badly.
Some nights still hurt. But she stopped reading their old chats, and one morning she realised she had gone a whole day without checking whether Noa had posted.

qa.q: Where did Noa want to move for good?
qa.a: Noa wanted to move to Berlin for good.

qa.q: What did the second list reveal to Nadia, and how did it make her feel?
qa.a: Nadia felt surprised and a little steadier, seeing that staying near family and talking about plans were real needs in a partner.

qa.q: What small steps helped Nadia recover, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the drafts, running with Inês and not reading old chats helped, because they broke the habit of reaching back and filled the time with support.

qa.q: How might Noa have felt ending a relationship where neither was wrong?
qa.a: Noa probably felt sad and torn too, but clear that staying would mean one of them giving up something important.

grounding: Shows a young adult recovering from a breakup caused by different life values and clarifying what she needs in a partner.

In the college library, between the tall shelves, Thomas finally said it. "Shalini, would you want to go out sometime? Like, on a date."
Shalini closed her book slowly. "Thomas, I really like you as a friend. But I don't feel that way. I'm sorry."
His face went hot. He had rehearsed everything except this answer. For a second he wanted to make a joke, or say he was only kidding.
Instead he nodded. "Okay. Thanks for being honest. Still friends for the stats assignment?"
She smiled, relieved. "Obviously."
That evening he went for a long walk round the campus lake and let himself feel rotten. He texted his older brother, who called back and listened. He didn't text Shalini for a few days, just to give himself space. When they met for the assignment, it was awkward for ten minutes, and then it wasn't.

qa.a: In the college library, between the tall shelves.

qa.a: Thomas felt embarrassed and hurt, his face going hot, and was briefly tempted to joke it away.

Seema Didi,
You asked how I'm doing since Priti and I broke up. Better, honestly. It's been two months.
At first I kept replaying it. Everyone thought we were perfect: same college, same jokes. But every time we talked about the future, it was a fight. She wanted a big city job and a life that moved fast. I want to come back to Nashik and help run Papa's workshop, and I want time. We kept pretending that didn't matter.
You told me to write down what I actually value. I did. Family close by. Honesty about money and plans. Kindness when tired. Priti had some of that, but we wanted different lives, and that's not a small thing.
I've stopped checking her profile. I'm playing cricket again on Sundays.
Next time, I'll talk about the future on the third date, not the third year.
Santosh

Salma's wedding was fixed for after Eid, in their small town near Imphal, and she was scared to ask anyone the questions in her head. Her mother only said, "Everything will be fine."
Lalremsiami, her friend from college who now worked at the district health centre, came to visit. On the roof, drying chillies, Salma finally asked, "Is it wrong if I'm not ready on the first night?"

Salma let out a long breath. "Can I bring him to talk to her?"

At a crowded house party in Mexico City, Camila noticed her friend Rania leaning hard against the wall, eyes half-closed. A guy Camila barely knew had his arm around her and was steering her toward a bedroom. "She's fine, she wants to lie down," he said.
Rania mumbled something that wasn't a word.
Camila stepped in front of them. "She can't decide anything like this. I'm taking her." Her heart was pounding. He shrugged, annoyed, and walked off.

Next morning, Rania didn't remember much. When Camila told her, she went quiet, then said, "Thank you for not deciding I was fine."

After finishing college, Pranav came back to his family's house in Satara and took a job at the town's co-operative bank. His father, Nitin, still decided everything: when the house was painted, who got invited to dinner, even which shirt Pranav wore to work.

Lucia had moved into a small flat in Madrid in September. Her father, Alejandro, had a key "for emergencies". By October, the emergencies included dropping off soup, fixing a tap she hadn't mentioned, and once waiting on her sofa when she came home late from work.

He laughed. "Invited. Very formal."
The next Wednesday he rang the bell, holding soup.

Thursday, 11 p.m.
It's Reena. I've been writing "tired" in this diary for two months. I counted tonight: fifty-three times.
It's not normal tired. I sleep ten hours and wake up heavy. I've stopped going to dance practice, which I used to love. I left the group chat on mute. I cry in the hostel bathroom and don't know why. When Manjula Aunty, my warden, asked if I was okay, I said "exams", even though exams finished two weeks ago.
The college health poster says: if low mood or exhaustion lasts more than two weeks, talk to someone. It's been eight.
So today I booked an appointment with the campus counsellor for tomorrow at ten. Then I went to Manjula Aunty's room and told her the truth. She made me tea and said she'll walk me there.
I'm scared. But I'm less alone than this morning.

passage:
Week 1: Chaitanya downloaded a cricket betting app "just for fun" during the season. He won a little on the first night and texted Seema, "Easy money."
Week 4: He was on it every night, chasing losses, hiding his phone when Seema came over. He'd borrowed from two friends. He snapped at her when she asked what was wrong.
Week 6: Seema found him sitting on his bike outside the hostel at midnight, shaking. "I keep telling myself one more win and I'll stop. It never happens."
She didn't lecture. She said, "This is a loop, not a character flaw. Let's get you out."
That night he deleted the app and blocked his card for betting sites. The next morning he told his elder brother and called a gambling helpline number from the college counselling centre, with Seema sitting beside him.

qa.q: What kind of app did Chaitanya download?
qa.a: A cricket betting app.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling at midnight in week 6?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt trapped and desperate, shaking because he couldn't stop despite promising himself.

qa.q: What steps helped Chaitanya start to exit the loop, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the app, blocking betting on his card, telling his brother and calling a helpline, because they cut off access and brought in support.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt watching the change from week 1 to week 6?
qa.a: Seema was probably worried and hurt by his snapping, but cared enough to stay calm and help.

grounding: Shows over several weeks how a betting habit became a dependence loop and the first steps to exit it.

passage:
Trisha, you asked why I don't drink at weddings. Let me tell you.
In my second year of college, I started drinking at hostel parties to feel less shy. Then before parties, to get ready. Then alone, on Sunday nights, to stop feeling anxious about Monday. I told myself I was fine because I still got good marks.
One morning I woke up and couldn't remember how I'd got back to my room. My roommate, Nisha, was sitting on her bed, waiting. She said, "I was really scared last night."
That did it. I went to the college counsellor that week. She helped me see the loop: anxiety, drink, relief, worse anxiety. I joined a support group and found other ways to calm down: running, and calling my sister.
It took more than a year. So when your Shreya Mausi says no thanks, that's why.

qa.q: What was Shreya's roommate's name?
qa.a: Nisha.

qa.q: How did young Shreya feel when she couldn't remember getting back to her room?
qa.a: Young Shreya felt frightened and shaken, realising things had gone too far.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why?
qa.a: Nisha saying she was scared, because it showed Shreya the harm to others and led her to the counsellor that week.

qa.q: What was that night like for Nisha?
qa.a: Nisha was probably terrified and helpless, sitting up waiting for her friend to wake.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting how drinking became a dependence loop in college and how she got out with help.

passage:
Mahima had three days left before her final exams, and she couldn't stop playing an online strategy game. Every time she opened her notes, her hand went to the laptop. "One match" became four hours. She was sleeping at 5 a.m. The hostel was quiet, her phone full of game alerts, and there was no one to stop her.
On the second night, her roommate Sonali found her crying at the desk. "I can't stop. I've tried."
Sonali didn't laugh. "Okay. What if I keep your laptop in my locker till Friday? And we study in the library together?"
Mahima hesitated. It felt childish. Then she handed it over and deleted the game from her phone.
The first day her hands kept reaching for nothing. By Friday she'd slept properly twice. After the exams, she booked an appointment with the college counsellor to work out why the game had such a hold.

qa.q: Where did Sonali offer to keep Mahima's laptop?
qa.a: In her locker till Friday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Sonali found her?
qa.a: Mahima felt helpless and ashamed, crying because she couldn't stop despite trying.

qa.q: Why was handing over the laptop and seeing a counsellor a good combination?
qa.a: Removing access got her through the exams, and the counsellor can help her understand and change the loop for the long term.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt finding Mahima crying at the desk?
qa.a: Sonali was probably worried and sympathetic, and wanted to offer practical help rather than judgement.

grounding: Shows a young adult caught in a gaming dependence loop under exam pressure and taking steps, with help, to exit it.

passage:
In my second year, my friends and I went to a wedding in my village. At dinner, my uncle seated the family's farm workers in a separate row, away from the "guests". Some of my college friends laughed and said nothing. I said nothing too.
Pema, my friend from Sikkim, noticed. On the bus back, Pema asked, "Did that feel right to you?"
It didn't. It hadn't for years. I just never said it, because it was family.
That night I made a list of things I'd stand by even if my family or friends didn't. Equality at my own table was first. Honesty was second.
At my cousin's engagement last month, I sat with the workers' families and ate with them. My uncle frowned. My mother didn't say anything, but later she brought me more rice. I'm Gurpreet, and I'm still working out the rest of the list.

qa.q: Where did the uncle seat the farm workers?
qa.a: In a separate row, away from the "guests".

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when Pema asked, "Did that feel right to you?"
qa.a: Gurpreet felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, admitting it hadn't felt right for years.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurpreet as the list grows?
qa.a: Keep testing each value in real moments, like the engagement, and accept that some family members may disagree.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother have felt bringing more rice?
qa.a: The mother may have felt quietly proud or supportive, even if she didn't want to challenge the uncle openly.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult defining a personal non-negotiable value independent of family custom and peers.

passage:
Internship supervisor's note. Aparna, NGO field projects.
Raghav joined us for a summer survey on water access in six villages. On day ten, some team members were behind and suggested filling in the last forty forms "based on what we already know". The deadline from the donor was close.
Raghav refused, politely but firmly. He said he'd come to the NGO because he believed the data should be true, and that fake data could send tankers to the wrong village. He offered to do extra field visits over the weekend instead.
I noticed he was nervous; his voice shook in the team meeting. The others were annoyed with him for a day.
He completed his forms by Monday. I've asked him to help me design a better schedule for the next survey. I've also told the team clearly that invented data is not acceptable here.

qa.q: How many forms did some team members suggest filling in without visits?
qa.a: The last forty forms.

qa.q: What does Raghav's shaking voice suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Raghav felt nervous and anxious about standing against the team, but determined to act on his values.

qa.q: How did Aparna support Raghav's stand?
qa.a: Aparna gave him responsibility for the next schedule and told the team clearly that invented data is not acceptable.

qa.q: How might the villagers be affected by Raghav's choice?
qa.a: They are more likely to get water help where it's truly needed, because the data about their access is real.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding to honesty as a non-negotiable value under peer and deadline pressure.

passage:
Sunday night
Sharmila writing. Everyone at lunch decided my life again. Mama says Uncle's firm will hire me after graduation, good salary, "settled". Nikita, my best friend, thinks I'm mad not to jump at it.
But I spent last summer at the children's library project and I've never felt so awake.
Tonight I wrote down what I actually want my life to stand for, not what anyone else wants:
1. Work that helps someone directly.
2. Honesty, even when awkward.
3. Enough money to be independent, not to impress anyone.
4. Time for my family.
Uncle's firm fits 3 and 4. The library job fits 1, 2 and 4, and maybe 3 if I'm careful.
I'm not deciding tonight. But I'm going to tell Mama tomorrow that I'll choose based on this list, not on who is loudest.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila spend last summer?
qa.a: At the children's library project.

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel about the family's lunch discussion?
qa.a: Sharmila feels frustrated and pressured, with everyone deciding for Sharmila.

qa.q: What is useful about Sharmila's list, and what would help next?
qa.a: It turns vague pressure into clear values to compare options against; talking it through with Mama and perhaps a careers mentor would help next.

qa.q: How might Nikita react on seeing the list?
qa.a: Nikita might still disagree, but could understand that Sharmila's choice comes from real values, not stubbornness.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult writing down personal values to decide independently of family and peer pressure.

passage:
In their small town in Kashmir, the results of the state service exam came out on a Tuesday. Dilnaz hadn't cleared the cut-off, for the second time. She went straight to her room and lay facing the wall.
"Two years wasted. Everyone was right about me," she said when her sister Rashmi came in.
Rashmi sat on the edge of the bed. "Who is everyone?"
"Me, mostly."
"Okay. Would you talk to me like that if I failed?"
Dilnaz was silent.
"So let's be honest, not cruel," Rashmi said. "What went wrong?"
Dilnaz thought. "I kept studying old topics I liked. I skipped current affairs. And I never did full mock tests."
"That's fixable."
That evening Dilnaz wrote a new plan. At the top she wrote: "I failed this exam. I am not a failure." Then she made a timetable.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz write at the top of her new plan?
qa.a: "I failed this exam. I am not a failure."

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she lay facing the wall?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt crushed and ashamed, believing her two years were wasted and that everyone had been right about her.

qa.q: What was helpful about Rashmi's approach?
qa.a: She challenged the cruel self-talk without pretending nothing went wrong, and helped Dilnaz name specific, fixable mistakes.

qa.q: What is it like for Rashmi to see her sister like this?
qa.a: Rashmi was probably sad and worried, but calm, wanting Dilnaz to be honest without being cruel to herself.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult shifting from harsh self-criticism to accountable, supportive self-talk after failing an exam.

passage:
In her first job at a design studio in Stockholm, Ingrid missed a client deadline because she'd misread the date. The client was annoyed. Her manager was polite but clearly disappointed.
That evening she walked home in the snow repeating, "You're so stupid. They'll never trust you again."
Her colleague Aiko caught up with her at the tram stop. "You look like you're punishing yourself."
"I am. I deserve it."
"You messed up a date. What will you do about it?"
Ingrid stopped. "Apologise to the client properly. Set calendar reminders two days before every deadline. Ask for a check-in for the next project."
"Good. Now say that instead of the stupid part."
Ingrid laughed shakily. On the tram, she wrote the apology email. Then she wrote a note for her desk: "Mistake, fixed, learned." She still felt bad. But she slept.

qa.q: What note did Ingrid write for her desk?
qa.a: "Mistake, fixed, learned."

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling as she walked home?
qa.a: Ingrid felt ashamed and harsh towards herself, repeating that she was stupid and would never be trusted again.

qa.q: What steps show accountable self-talk rather than just being nice to herself?
qa.a: Apologising properly to the client, setting reminders two days before deadlines and asking for a check-in, while dropping the insults.

qa.q: How might Aiko see Ingrid after the tram-stop talk?
qa.a: Aiko probably sees Ingrid as someone who made a normal mistake and handled it well, and feels glad to have helped.

grounding: Shows a young adult replacing harsh self-criticism after a work mistake with accountable, supportive self-talk.
